The overall increase of $5.0 million for the 12 special political missions is attributable primarily to: (a) an increase of $3.8 million under civilian personnel, owing to the application of lower vacancy rates and revised salary rates; and (b) and increase of $1.2 million under operational costs, mainly due to the provisioning of a full year in 2027, compared to nine months budgeted in 2026, for the Office of the Special Envoy for Yemen following the transfer as of 1 April 2026 of residual tasks previously performed by the United Nations Mission to Support the Hudaydah Agreement (UNMHA) pursuant to Security Council resolution 2813 (2026) of requirements under air operations for the rental and operation of one fixed-wing aircraft, and under facilities and infrastructure for the rental of premises and security services. The increase was offset in part by: (a) reduced requirements under communications and information technology, owing to lower needs for the acquisition of equipment and reduced subscription costs for periodicals and publications; and (b) reduced requirements under ground transportation, owing to lower needs for rental of vehicles and spare parts.
Vacancy rates

The proposed vacancy rates applied in the budget take into account the experience to date. The assumptions considered for the proposed vacancy factors include: (a) the 12-month average vacancy rate from January to December in 2025; and (b) the actual vacancy rate as at 31 March 2026. The lower of the two was used as the budgeted vacancy rate. This is in line with the policy guidance to improve the accuracy and consistency of the vacancy factors applied in the proposed budgets for 2027 and to ensure that the proposed vacancy rates are based, as much as possible, on actual rates. For the Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Yemen, the proposed vacancy rates reflect their planned deployment during the period, taking into account the encumbrance of the new positions established as of 1 April 2026 by staff previously funded under UNMHA, reflecting a cost-effective arrangement to ensure operational continuity. A vacancy rate of 50 per cent has been applied in the calculation of costs for the posts proposed for establishment. Annex II outlines the proposed vacancy rates for 2027.
Efficiency gains

The proposed budget reflects efficiencies and cost-reductions measures, resulting in reduced requirements for civilian personnel and operational costs. Civilian personnel requirements are reduced primarily as a result of: (a)  the proposed abolishment of one Under-Secretary-General level post in the Office of Support for the implementation of Security Council resolution 1559 (2004); (b) the proposed downward reclassification of one D-1 post to the P-5 level in the Office of the Special Envoy for Syria; and (c) the proposed relocation of one P-3 post from Geneva to New York under the Office of the United Nations Representative to the Geneva International Discussions. In addition, requirements  for  operational costs are reduced primarily owing to efficiencies achieved under the following classes of expenditures: (a) communications and information technology, in the Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for the Great Lakes Region, reflecting lower subscription costs for periodicals following  the shift to a cost-sharing arrangement for electronic resources with the Dag Hammarskjöld Library, replacing individual subscriptions; (b) ground transportation, resulting from the transition to electric vehicles in the Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for the Great Lakes Region, leading to reduced fuel consumption and maintenance requirements; (c) official travel, where additional savings are expected from increased use of virtual meetings and  consolidation of travel itineraries in the Mission of the Secretary-General’s Good Offices in Cyprus and the Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for the Great Lakes Region; (d) facilities and infrastructure, resulting from the replacement of conventional light bulbs with energy-efficient alternatives, in the Mission of the Secretary-General’s Good Offices in Cyprus; and (e) other supplies, services and equipment, reflecting savings from an increased number of online meetings, and a reduced need for interpretation services due to meetings conducted using a single working language in the Mission of the Secretary-General’s Good Offices in Cyprus.

children.text: Extrabudgetary resources
For the sake of brevity, the present document will include a section on extrabudgetary resources only for those missions that have projected extrabudgetary resources in 2026 or 2027.
Gender perspective

Special political missions are guided by the relevant Security Council resolutions2F on the women and peace and security agenda, which mandate the incorporation of a gender perspective into the political work of the United Nations, including in special political missions. The missions are also guided by General Assembly resolution 75/100 on the comprehensive review of special political missions, in which the Assembly reaffirmed the important role of women in the prevention and resolution of conflicts and in peacebuilding and recognized the importance of the equal and effective participation and the full involvement of women at all levels, at all stages and in all aspects of the peaceful settlement of disputes, conflict prevention and conflict resolution.

Specific examples of how special political missions integrate a gender perspective into their operational activities, deliverables and results are given under the individual missions in the present report.
Disability inclusion

In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, special political missions review the Strategy with a view to further advancing disability inclusion through inclusive messaging, awareness-raising and promoting the Strategy through their work, including in political and peace processes. The missions also support mitigating measures to overcome accessibility challenges, in addition to the efforts by relevant United Nations entities to ensure the accessibility of facilities, platforms, security and other infrastructure to facilitate easy access and use by persons with disabilities.
Evaluation activities

In 2025, the Office of Internal Oversight Services completed an evaluation of conflict specific special political missions under thematic cluster I to assess the relevance, effectiveness and coherence of their contributions to mitigating the risk of violent conflict. The findings of the evaluation have informed the proposed programme plans for the missions for 2027.

In response to the evaluation results, missions will strengthen their strategic planning to better adapt to changes in mandate and evolving operational conditions, considering their respective capacities. Missions will also integrate greater inclusivity into their activities to further enhance their effectiveness and responsiveness. In addition, they will identify lessons learned and best practices by improving knowledge processes and information sharing.
Mission specific evaluation activities, where applicable, are described under the respective missions in the present report.
1.	Mission of the Secretary-General’s Good Offices in Cyprus
A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

The mandate of the mission derives from the priorities established in relevant Security Council resolutions and decisions and an exchange of letters between the Secretary-General and the President of the Security Council (S/2008/456 and S/2008/457). In resolution 1818 (2008), the Council welcomed the intention of the Secretary-General to appoint a Special Adviser, and, in a letter addressed to the President of the Security Council (S/2008/456), the Secretary-General announced his intention to appoint his Special Adviser on Cyprus as from 14 July 2008. Relevant Security Council resolutions from which the mandate derives include resolution 186 (1964) and various subsequent Council resolutions, the latest being resolution 2815 (2026).

The position of the Special Adviser was discontinued as of 1 January 2026 following the approval by the General Assembly of the proposal made in the revised estimates for the 2026 programme budget (A/80/400). Accordingly, the name of the mission is adjusted, from the Office of the Special Adviser of the Secretary General on Cyprus, to the current name.

In its resolution 2815 (2026), the Security Council fully supported the Secretary-General’s ongoing engagement and welcomed the intensification of dialogue. The Council welcomed the Secretary-General’s convening of informal broader meetings in March and July 2025 with the two sides and the guarantor powers, emphasized the importance of negotiating a mutually acceptable settlement under United Nations auspices and strongly called upon the sides to engage actively with the Secretary-General and his team to that end. The Council also called on the two leaders to empower the Technical Committees.
Programme of work
Objective
The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to achieve a comprehensive settlement of the Cyprus issue.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, the mission will:
Support the two leaders and guarantor powers to promote a peaceful solution and to assist them, should they jointly agree, in the conduct of full-fledged negotiations;

Regularly conduct bilateral meetings and facilitate joint meetings between the leaders and their representatives, emphasizing the importance of effective communication for conflict prevention and trust-building;
Support the implementation of confidence- and trust-building measures and initiatives and the work of the technical committees.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:
Dialogue among the parties resulting in further rounds of talks towards a comprehensive and just settlement in Cyprus;
Meetings and the expansion of bicommunal contacts;
Empowerment and facilitation of the work of the technical committees, resulting in concrete measures and the implementation of confidence-building measures and trust-building initiatives.

With regard to cooperation with other entities, the mission will coordinate the engagement of international financial institutions in support of the peace process and cooperate with the European Commission, when requested. The mission has gained efficiencies by leveraging support from the European Commission, in particular to the 13 technical committees, through an European Union-funded support facility for the activities of the committees.

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the mission, the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus and the United Nations country team will maximize synergies and ensure coherent and effective support for peace efforts, especially for mandated activities in support to the technical committees.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
Continued and sustained political commitment of the parties to the peace process and the technical committees;
Continued and sustained international support for the peace process.

The mission integrates a gender perspective into its activities, and advocates for gender equality in the peace process and across the work of all technical committees. It also advocates for greater civic inclusion and the involvement of youth and underrepresented groups.

In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the mission will further mainstream disability inclusion into its work, advocate for the inclusion of persons with disabilities in engagement with the sides and the technical committees and ensure accessibility and employment opportunities for qualified candidates with disabilities.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 initiative

The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects efforts of the mission to implement all mandates in a more efficient and effective manner and contains no substantive adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative.
Evaluation activities

In 2025, the evaluation completed by Office of Internal Oversight Services (OIOS) found that the facilitation of the technical committees was deemed effective by both sides and contributed to fostering engagement, mutual understanding and tangible bi-communal initiatives. The mission illustrated some good practices that facilitated dialogue and helped to build trust between the parties, and was recognized as the only interlocutor working on the Cyprus peace process that was able to engage the two parties on an equal basis.

In response to the evaluation, the mission will continue the practices recognized by OIOS that facilitated dialogue and helped to build trust in its work on the peace process. The mission will continue its regular engagements with the diplomatic community and with various local and international civil society organizations and continue to improve meaningful engagement with youth and other underrepresented groups.
In 2027, the mission plans to conduct an internal evaluation of its external communication strategy and activities.
Programme performance in 2025

The establishment of the Technical Committee on Youth, together with other trust-building initiatives, strengthened dialogue, reduced tensions and raised hope among Cypriots, improving their situation vis-à-vis prospects for peace process

At the broader-format informal meeting with the guarantor powers on 17 and 18 March 2025, hosted by the Secretary-General, the parties agreed on six trust-building initiatives, including the establishment of a new technical committee on youth. A further broader-format meeting in July 2025 resulted in additional four initiatives agreed to build trust. The Secretary-General hosted the two leaders again in September 2025, and the United Nations facilitated meetings in November and December 2025 and as of May 2026, four additional leaders’ meetings were held. While the number of meetings with the leaders and their negotiating teams in 2025 remained comparable to 2024, the number of meetings and the outputs of the technical committees increased, including in quality, with projects that improved the daily lives of Cypriots.

children.text: Planned result for 2027
Furthering dialogue as a conflict management tool and an inclusive and sustainable peace process towards a negotiated settlement – Programme performance in 2025 and target for 2027

In 2025, the mission’s work contributed to the holding of and support to 63 bilateral and joint meetings with the leaders and their representatives and 358 meetings of the technical committees, falling short of the planned target of 140 and 410 meetings, respectively. This shortfall stemmed primarily from the absence of active negotiations and the shift toward planning for the high-level meetings with the two sides and guarantor powers. In addition, no meetings at the level of the two leaders were held during the pre-election campaign period preceding the change in leadership in the Turkish Cypriot community in October 2025.

In 2027, the Mission will focus on the support to high-level meetings, trust-building activities, the work of the technical committees and the use of dialogue as an effective early warning and conflict prevention tool. Amid a persistent challenging regional landscape, additional trust-building measures to benefit Cypriots across the island for 2026 and 2027 will also be pursued.
Lessons learned and planned change

The lesson learned in 2025 was that despite tangible progress on trust building initiatives, including those delegated to the technical committees, public attention focused on measures not yet implemented, negatively impacting the atmosphere between the two communities. Considering its unique role in bridging divides, building trust and fostering cooperation in Cyprus, as underscored by the OIOS evaluation, the mission will strengthen its planning tools to improve effectiveness and responsiveness, particularly regarding the technical committees as trust-building bodies. Once trust-building initiatives have received the necessary political support for implementation, the mission will also help the technical committees shorten implementation timelines.

2.	Office of the Special Adviser to the Secretary-General on the Prevention of Genocide
A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

The mission is mandated to collect information on massive and serious violations of human rights and international humanitarian law of ethnic and racial origin that, if not prevented or halted, may lead to genocide; to act as a mechanism of early warning to the Secretary-General and, through him, to the Security Council, by bringing to their attention situations that could potentially result in genocide; to make recommendations to the Council, through the Secretary-General, on action to prevent or halt genocide; and to liaise with the United Nations system on activities for the prevention of genocide and on work to enhance the capacity of the United Nations to analyse and manage information regarding genocide or related crimes.

The mandate derives from the invitation of the Security Council to the Secretary-General in its resolution 1366 (2001) to refer to the Council information and analysis from within the United Nations system on cases of serious violations of international law, including international humanitarian law and human rights law. The Special Adviser on the Prevention of Genocide was appointed through an exchange of letters between the Secretary-General and the President of the Security Council (S/2004/567 and S/2004/568). The responsibilities of the Special Adviser were listed in the letter of the Secretary-General (S/2004/567). The mandate has been reaffirmed through various resolutions of the Security Council,3F the General Assembly4F and the Human Rights Council.5F In its resolution 77/318, the General Assembly noted the role of the Special Adviser in the launch of the United Nations Strategy and Plan of Action on Hate Speech and as part of efforts to address and counter hate speech.

With regard to the responsibility to protect, the General Assembly, in paragraphs 138 and 139 of its resolution 60/1 on the 2005 World Summit Outcome, addressed the responsibility of Member States and the international community to protect populations from genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity. The Security Council reaffirmed the provisions of paragraphs 138 and 139 of that resolution in its resolutions 1674 (2006) and 1706 (2006). Through an exchange of letters (S/2007/721 and S/2007/722), the Special Adviser to the Secretary-General on the Responsibility to Protect was appointed and charged with the conceptual, institutional and operational development of the principle and with continuing a political dialogue with Member States on its implementation. The Assembly, in resolution 75/277, included an item on the responsibility to protect in its agenda and requested the Secretary-General to report annually on that item.

In its resolutions 2150 (2014) and 2171 (2014), the Security Council recalled the important role of the Special Advisers on the Prevention of Genocide and on the Responsibility to Protect, whose functions included acting as an early warning mechanism to prevent situations that could result in genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and ethnic cleansing.

Designated by the Secretary-General as the United Nations focal point for the implementation of the United Nations Strategy and Plan of Action on Hate Speech, launched in 2019, the mission recognizes hate speech as a risk factor and indicator for genocide. The importance of addressing hate speech, and the Special Adviser’s role, has been underscored in numerous United Nations resolutions, including General Assembly resolutions 75/309 and 77/318 and Security Council resolution 2686 (2023). Furthermore, the General Assembly, in its resolution 78/282, requested the Secretary-General to establish an outreach programme entitled “The Srebrenica Genocide and the United Nations”, starting its activities with preparations for the commemoration of the thirtieth anniversary of the genocide in 2025, and to bring the resolution to the attention of all Member States, organizations of the United Nations system and civil society organizations for appropriate observance.
Programme of work
Objective

The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to advance national, regional and international efforts to protect populations from genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity and their incitement.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, the mission will:

Raise awareness of the causes and dynamics of genocide through predictive and action-oriented analysis, enhanced by the collection and sharing of information from field missions and regional offices in accordance with its early warning mandate;
Alert relevant actors with respect to the risk of genocide, through the implementation of the United Nations Strategy and Plan of Action on Hate Speech, capacity-building and advocacy;
Advocate and mobilize for appropriate action to prevent the risk of genocide through engagement within the United Nations and with external partners;
Strengthen community-level efforts for prevention, including by assisting locally led initiatives aimed at bringing communities together;
Harness technology to enhance prevention and counter its negative impacts, as outlined in Human Rights Council resolution 49/9;

Increase female participation in decision-making roles and support implementation of the plan of action for women in communities to counter hate speech and prevent incitement to violence that could lead to genocide and related crimes;
Prioritize action against Holocaust and genocide denial and the glorification of war crimes and criminals;

Support the universal ratification of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide and support efforts towards its implementation at the national level through legislation and implementation mechanisms.

The above-mentioned work is expected to result in increased capacity and action by United Nations intergovernmental bodies, Member States and regional and subregional organizations to prevent and mitigate the risk of genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity, including their incitement.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:

Continued commitment of Member States, the Security Council and other intergovernmental bodies to engage with the mission to advance the prevention of genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity, including through conceptual development and consensus-building on the nature of the responsibility to protect;

Active engagement of Member States and regional and other organizations to develop preventive capacity and take appropriate action for the prevention of genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity, including their incitement.

With regard to cooperation with other entities, the mission will continue to work and partner with regional organizations, including the African Union, the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region, the Economic Community of West African States, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), the Organization of American States, the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) and the European Union, among others, as well as with civil society, including religious leaders, traditional leaders, academia and traditional media, on developing capacity and taking appropriate action for the prevention of genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity, including their incitement, at the national, regional and local levels.

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the mission works closely with and supports United Nations country teams on the implementation of the United Nations Strategy and Plan of Action on Hate Speech.

The mission integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate. This includes reflecting the gender dynamics in its monitoring and analysis and striving for the equal participation of women in its capacity-building events and workshops.

In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the mission has developed and implements a guidance note on integrating disability inclusion into its programmes and activities to ensure that its work systematically incorporates the rights and needs of persons with disabilities.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 initiative

The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects changes arising from the UN80 Initiative. In particular, the tables of deliverables reflect updated planned deliverables for 2026, in line with the approved programme budget for 2026.
Programme performance in 2025
Strengthened genocide prevention capacities of regional organizations, governments, non-governmental organizations and civil society organizations

In 2025, the mission supported the Uganda National Committee for the Prevention of Genocide and Other Mass Atrocities, enabling a two‑day workshop to revitalize the Committee after two years of inactivity and prepare an action plan ahead of the January 2026 elections in Uganda. The workshop facilitated the Committee’s election of its new leadership bureau and enhanced members’ capacity to assess and respond to risks of genocide and other atrocity crimes. As a result, new leaders were elected, members received targeted training on prevention, and a practical action plan was developed to guide the Committee’s work during and after the elections. During the elections, the Committee deployed observers and produced a report with recommendations to mitigate election‑related violence, which the Special Adviser shared with relevant UN entities. This experience highlights the value of the mission’s support in strengthening national mechanisms for genocide and atrocity‑crime prevention.

Building on sustained technical engagement, the mission also strengthened its prevention framework through the development and adoption of three policy documents and training manuals in 2025. Focused on countering hate speech and enhancing genocide prevention, these resources provide communities, non-governmental organizations (NGO), and civil society organizations with tools for risk identification and response. As a result, vulnerable communities benefit from stronger risk analysis, more coordinated prevention strategies, and increased resilience to genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity. Combined with increased advocacy following General Assembly resolution 78/282 on the Srebrenica genocide commemoration, these advances reinforce global prevention efforts and support healing processes for affected communities.

Enhanced protection from atrocity crimes through improved awareness and prevention mechanisms and better risk identification capabilities for Member States and regional organizations – Programme performance in 2025 and target for 2027

In 2025, the mission advanced national, regional and international efforts to protect populations from genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity, and met the planned target of 20 follow‑up actions taken by Member States and regional organizations to address risks of such crimes. A special emphasis was placed on supporting the revitalization of prevention of genocide work within the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR), reinforcing regional commitment to early warning and coordinated prevention efforts.
Lessons learned and planned change

The lesson for the mission was that collaborating with United Nations field entities, NGOs and civil society organizations proved essential in improving outreach and strengthening the quality of risk assessments. Joint development of context‑specific action plans enhanced partners’ capacity to detect and respond to hate‑speech trends, while memorandums of understanding with civil society organizations improved access to timely community‑level information. Going forward, the mission will deepen collaboration, information‑sharing and joint analysis with community level and regional partners to strengthen the assessment of risks related to genocide and other atrocity crimes.

At the same time, to respond to evolving risks of genocide and other atrocity crimes, the mission adjusted its delivery modalities by shifting from predominantly knowledge-product outputs to more practice‑oriented workshops, strengthening engagement with United Nations country teams, and expanding the use of virtual platforms, thereby enhancing reach, responsiveness, and impact in support of its prevention objectives.

3.	Personal Envoy of the Secretary-General for Western Sahara
A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

The Personal Envoy of the Secretary-General for Western Sahara is responsible for assisting the parties, Morocco and the Frente Popular para la Liberación de Saguía el-Hamra y de Río de Oro (Frente POLISARIO), in finding a just, lasting and mutually acceptable political solution, which will provide for the self-determination of the people of Western Sahara in the context of arrangements consistent with the principles and purposes of the Charter of the United Nations.

The mandate derives from the communications between the Secretary-General and the President of the Security Council dated 17 March 1997 (S/1997/236), 1 October 2021 (S/2021/851) and 5 October 2021 (S/2021/852), as well as from the priorities established through Security Council resolutions. Most recently, in its resolution 2797 (2025), the Council expressed its full support for the Secretary-General and his Personal Envoy in facilitating and conducting negotiations and called upon the parties to engage in these discussions without preconditions, taking as basis Morocco’s Autonomy Proposal, with a view to achieving a final and mutually acceptable political solution that provides for the self-determination of the people of Western Sahara.
Programme of work
Objective

The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to advance the parties’ efforts to achieve a just, lasting and mutually acceptable political solution, which will provide for the self-determination of the people of Western Sahara.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, the mission will:

Encourage the parties to continue the discussion on the question of Western Sahara in order to identify elements of convergence, through bilateral consultations, including with the neighbouring countries of Algeria and Mauritania, conduct visits to the region to meet with key interlocutors and engage in shuttle diplomacy and other activities deemed useful in that regard;
Consult with members of the Security Council and the Group of Friends on Western Sahara, both in their capitals and in New York, as well as with regional organizations, towards a solution;
Facilitate two international meetings bringing together all concerned on Western Sahara.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:
Additional trust built and strengthened involvement by the parties in the political process;
Maintained support by the international community for the political process.
With regard to cooperation with other entities, the mission regularly meets with regional organizations and other relevant stakeholders to exchange views on the United Nations-led political process.

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the mission receives support for visits and information on developments in Western Sahara from the United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara. It also coordinates and liaises with the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees on visits to the refugee camps and on confidence-building measures and maintains contact with the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights in Geneva on issues related to the human rights situation.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
All concerned show willingness to meet for direct negotiations;
The security situation remains conducive to the mission’s objective for the region.

The mission integrates a gender perspective into its activities. It ensures that women and representatives of women’s organizations are included in meetings with civil society and will encourage delegations to include women in political meetings.
In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the mission will include consultations with persons with disabilities on their inclusion in meetings.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 initiative

The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects efforts of the mission to implement all mandates in a more efficient and effective manner and contains no substantive adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative.
Programme performance in 2025
Readiness of all concerned to engage

In 2025, renewed international engagement contributed to efforts of the United Nations to make progress in the political process led by the Personal Envoy. In this context, the Personal Envoy continued his efforts to engage all concerned and undertook broadened consultations on the issue of Western Sahara with a view to constructively advancing the political process. The consultations focused on exploring constructive suggestions for the people of Western Sahara to attain a just, lasting and mutually acceptable political solution that provides for their self-determination. The adoption of Security Council resolution 2797 on 31 October 2025, provided new impetus to efforts to resolve the conflict based on renewed international engagement in support of the political process. These developments contributed to a readiness of all concerned to engage with a view to resolving the protracted situation and meet the aspirations of the people of Western Sahara to find a just, lasting and mutually acceptable political solution that provides for the self-determination of the people of Western Sahara.

4.	Support for the implementation of Security Council resolution 1559 (2004)
A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

On 14 December 2004, the Secretary-General appointed his Special Envoy for the implementation of Security Council resolution 1559 (2004) to enable him to report to the Council every six months on the implementation of the resolution, as requested by the Council in its presidential statement of 19 October 2004 (S/PRST/2004/36).

In its resolution 1680 (2006), the Council reiterated its call for the full implementation of the provisions of resolution 1559 (2004), and strongly encouraged the Government of the Syrian Arab Republic to respond positively to the request made by the Government of Lebanon, in line with the agreements of the Lebanese national dialogue, to delineate their common border, especially in those areas where the border was uncertain or disputed.

In its resolution 1701 (2006), the Council emphasized the importance of the extension of the control of the Government of Lebanon over all Lebanese territory in accordance with the provisions of resolutions 1559 (2004) and 1680 (2006), and of the relevant provisions of the Taif Accords. The Council requested the Secretary-General to develop, in liaison with relevant international actors and the parties concerned, proposals to implement the relevant provisions of the Taif Accords and resolutions 1559 (2004) and 1680 (2006), including disarmament, and for delineation of the international borders of Lebanon.
In subsequent resolutions on Lebanon, the Council continued to urge all parties to make tangible progress towards all outstanding issues in the implementation of relevant Council resolutions.

In a statement by the President of the Security Council of 16 January 2025 (S/PRST/2025/1), the Council welcomed the cessation of hostilities arrangement between Israel and Lebanon of 26 November 2024 (S/2024/870). The Council called upon the parties to faithfully implement the provisions of the arrangement and for the full implementation of resolution 1701 (2006) and the Security Council’s previous relevant resolutions by all parties.

In 2016, the Under-Secretary-General for Political Affairs was tasked by the Secretary-General with assuming the responsibility of reporting on the implementation of resolution 1559 (2004), an arrangement that has been maintained to date.
Programme of work
Objective
The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to ensure full implementation of Security Council resolution 1559 (2004) and all subsequent related resolutions of the Council.
Strategy and external factors for 2027

To contribute to the objective, the mission will seek to support efforts to foster consensus on a Lebanese-led and Lebanese-owned national dialogue, which is expected to result in progress on addressing the maintenance of weapons outside State authority.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in informed Security Council deliberations on  progress made by Lebanon on the outstanding provisions of Council resolution 1559 (2004).

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the mission coordinates with the Office of the United Nations Special Coordinator for Lebanon, in particular in the process of developing the reports of the Secretary-General.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
The regional environment continues to affect Lebanon’s stability and security;

Following the 2026 legislative elections and the formation of a new government, the Lebanese leadership pursues efforts to deliver reforms and tangible benefits for the population as it faces reconstruction challenges;
The Lebanese government has reaffirmed its commitment to ensuring a State monopoly over the maintenance of weapons;
Member States within and outside the region remain engaged in supporting  the disbanding and disarmament of Lebanese and non-Lebanese militias;
Violations of Lebanese sovereignty and territorial integrity persist.

The mission integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities by ensuring appropriate consultations with all stakeholders, including women leaders, and the inclusion of gender-disaggregated data, as appropriate.

In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the mission will support mitigating measures to overcome accessibility challenges, in addition to the efforts undertaken by relevant United Nations entities to ensure the accessibility of facilities, platforms, security and other infrastructure to facilitate easy access and use by persons with disabilities.

The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects efforts of the mission to implement all mandates in a more efficient and effective manner and contains no substantive adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative.

5.	Office of the United Nations Representative to the Geneva International Discussions
A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

The mission is mandated to support the Geneva International Discussions and the Incident Prevention and Response Mechanism under United Nations auspices in Gali, Georgia, by facilitating the participation of the United Nations in the international discussions in Geneva and the Gali Incident Prevention and Response Mechanism, and by liaising and coordinating with the relevant actors. The mission is also responsible for preparing, convening and facilitating, in consultation with the other Co-Chairs, the European Union and the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), the sessions of the Geneva International Discussions as well as the periodic meetings of the Gali Incident Prevention and Response Mechanism.

The United Nations has continued to support the Geneva International Discussions on security and stability and the return of internally displaced persons and refugees, which commenced on 15 October 2008 in Geneva in accordance with the six-point agreement of 12 August 2008 and the implementing measures of 8 September 2008, mediated by the French presidency of the European Union, following the hostilities of August 2008 (S/2009/254). In its resolution 1866 (2009), the Security Council welcomed the beginning of the discussions and requested the Secretary-General, through his Special Representative, to continue to fully support the process. The Secretary-General addressed a letter on the matter to the Minister for Foreign Affairs of Georgia on 29 September 2009, and the Minister replied to the Secretary-General on 28 October 2009.

Against the background of the “Proposals for joint incident prevention and response mechanisms”, agreed to in Geneva on 18 February 2009, the Secretary-General, on 28 September 2009, addressed a letter to the President of the Security Council in which he stated that the United Nations would continue to support the Geneva International Discussions and the Mechanism through a limited number of personnel with the task of facilitating the United Nations participation in the international discussions in Geneva and in the Mechanism, and liaising and coordinating with the relevant actors.

In a letter dated 28 December 2009 addressed to the President of the Security Council, the Secretary-General noted that the United Nations would continue to provide support for the Geneva International Discussions and the work of the Mechanism. In a letter dated 25 February 2010 addressed to the President of the Security Council (S/2010/103), the Secretary-General conveyed his intention to appoint a United Nations Representative responsible for United Nations support for the Geneva International Discussions and the Mechanism. In a letter dated 2 May 2011 (S/2011/279), the President of the Security Council informed the Secretary-General that the members of the Security Council had taken note of his intention and of the information contained in his letter of 25 February 2010. In 2018, there was an additional exchange of letters between the Secretary-General and the President of the Security Council regarding the appointment of a United Nations Representative.

Currently, one Assistant Secretary-General in the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs discharges the responsibilities of the United Nations’s representative to the Geneva International Discussions.
Programme of work
Objective

The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to advance the main agenda items of the Geneva International Discussions, including the non-use of force/international security arrangements and addressing the issue of internally displaced persons and refugees, in the context of the Discussions and the Gali Incident Prevention and Response Mechanism.
Strategy and external factors for 2027

To contribute to the objective, the mission, in close partnership with the other Co-Chairs, will continue efforts to facilitate progress on key agenda items of the Discussions, and ensure that the regular meetings of the Gali Incident Prevention and Response Mechanism serve as results-oriented platforms for dialogue and conflict prevention.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:
Contributing to the objective of transitioning the Discussions from a conflict management to a conflict transformation and resolution process;
Addressing and making progress on central issues, including the non-use of force/international security arrangements and internally displaced persons and refugees.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
All stakeholders will continue to support the Discussions and the Gali Incident Prevention and Response Mechanism and the engagement of the United Nations;
All stakeholders will support efforts to enhance the effectiveness of the Discussions;
The Co-Chairs will continue to collaborate closely to fulfil the mandate of the Discussions.

With regard to cooperation with other entities, the mission coordinates with the European Union and OSCE Co-Chairs. It maintains contact with the European Union Monitoring Mission in Georgia and OSCE, which jointly facilitate the work of the Incident Prevention and Response Mechanism in Ergneti and other relevant actors.

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the mission cooperates closely with entities within the United Nations system so as to coordinate and strengthen the role and contribution of the United Nations within the framework of the Discussions and the Gali Incident Prevention and Response Mechanism, especially in addressing humanitarian issues.

The mission integrates a gender perspective into its activities, including engaging in advocacy for gender equality and promoting the role of women in conflict resolution and peacebuilding, including within the framework of the Co-Chairs’ joint strategy and action plan on women and peace and security.
The mission will closely cooperate with the United Nations Office at Geneva in the implementation of the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 initiative –

The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects efforts of the mission to implement all mandates in a more efficient and effective manner and contains no substantive adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative.
Programme performance in 2025
Continuation of efforts to achieve concrete results on key issues on the agenda of the Geneva International Discussions

Three rounds of the Discussions took place in 2025, on 4 and 5 March, 25 and 26 June and 11 and 12 November, respectively. The Co-Chairs organized three visits to Tbilisi, Moscow, Sukhumi and Tskhinvali, as well as Washington D.C., and New York. The Co-Chairs also briefed the OSCE Permanent Council in Vienna on 25 September 2025. In addition to traditional bilateral meetings with participants of the Geneva International Discussions rounds, the Co-Chairs, during the 64th round, conducted an information session on the issues of mobility and freedom of movement, inviting external experts, which was acknowledged by the participants. The mission undertook visits to Tbilisi, Zugdidi, Gali and Sukhumi to engage with relevant actors. Despite the mission’s efforts, no meetings of the Gali Incident Prevention and Response Mechanism took place due to persisting differences among key participants on the modalities. The mission will continue its efforts aimed at resumption of the Mechanism.

6.	Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Syria
A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

Established in 2012 as the Office of the Joint UN and Arab League Special Envoy for Syria, the United Nations Office of the Special Envoy for Syria has primarily focused on carrying out the activities mandated by Security Council resolution 2254 (2015). Other mandated priorities and tasks of the Office are contained in Security Council resolutions 2118 (2013), 2268 (2016) and 2336 (2016), as well as General Assembly resolution 66/253.

Since the developments of 8 December 2024, the Security Council has called for an inclusive, Syrian-led and owned political transition process grounded in the key principles of resolution 2254 (2015), as recalled in resolution 2799 (2025). The Council, as reflected in two Presidential Statements (S/PRST/2025/4 and S/PRST/2025/6), has reaffirmed the importance of the United Nations’ role in supporting this political transition process and has reiterated its support for the efforts of the Special Envoy in this regard.
Programme of work
Objective

The objective of this mission is to advance the full implementation of all the relevant General Assembly and Security Council resolutions towards an inclusive, credible, comprehensive Syrian-owned and -led political solution to the conflict in the Syrian Arab Republic that meets the legitimate aspirations of the Syrian people for dignity, freedom and justice, based on the principles of equality and non-discrimination and with the full and meaningful participation of women.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, the Mission will, in agreement with the Syrian government:
Offer its good offices to contribute to conflict prevention and resolution, supporting Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity;
Support national efforts for institutional reform;
Support the Syrian-led process of drafting a new permanent constitution that reflects a new social contract inclusive of all Syrian constituencies;
Assist the Syrian-led process of preparing inclusive, free, and fair elections;
Support the legislative work of the transitional Parliamentary Assembly;
Support the advancement of transitional justice, including through assistance in rule of law reform and national reconciliation;
Support economic recovery and reconstruction, including with a view to facilitating the return of Internally Displaced Persons (IDP) and refugees;
Support Syria’s economic recovery, including by addressing sanctions and other constraints;
Promote women’s meaningful political participation, including through community representation, and civic space for civil society to operate freely;
Advocate for the respect, protection and fulfilment of human rights of all Syrians, and promote accountability for serious violations and reparations for survivors;

Strengthen UN coordination across humanitarian, development, and peacebuilding pillars in support of the Syrian government and the Syrian people to enhance coherence, effectiveness, and impact across all UN activities in Syria.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:
Sustained, regular, and substantive dialogue with the Syrian government and the broadest possible spectrum of Syrian society on all key aspects of the political transition process;

A political transition process that integrates the perspectives of all Syrian constituencies at all stages, that fosters social cohesion, and that progressively provides a pathway to long-term, inclusive governance, based on a new constitution and free, fair elections;

Increased trust among all Syrian constituencies in the political transition process, supported by strong international consensus and conducted in a climate of national reconciliation, which is essential for lasting peace and stability;
Gradual economy  recovery that would facilitate returns of Syrians and economic development

Strengthened coordination among United Nations humanitarian, development and peacebuilding entities, and among regional and international actors, to ensure coherent support to the Syrian-led political transition, stabilization and recovery efforts.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:

National, regional and international stakeholders will show readiness to constructively engage and cooperate with the Office of the Special Envoy to advance common objectives, in a spirit of good faith and shared responsibility;

The country will continue to face substantial challenges related to national reconciliation, the establishment of state authority, security sector reform, respect for the rule of law, security threats, and violations of its sovereignty. Governance will therefore remain challenging but is expected to gradually evolve towards a more inclusive and stable political and institutional framework;
Processes for accountability and transitional justice will be accompanied by genuine efforts to promote social peace and national reconciliation among Syrians;

The Syrian economy will remain fragile, requiring sustained international financial and technical support throughout 2027 and beyond, along with continued adjustments to regulatory and institutional frameworks, including strengthening anti-corruption measures and transparency safeguards, to build investor and donor confidence and enable recovery and growth;

In 2027 the Mission will maintain operational flexibility to support its mandate from locations deemed most effective and appropriate, subject to the Government’s authorization and security considerations.

With regard to cooperation with other entities, the Mission will continue to engage with Syrian women and civil society and draw on their inputs and insights. In addition, the Mission will engage with, and as appropriate, offer support within its mandate to specialized Syrian and international bodies, including the Syrian national commissions for transitional justice and missing persons. Furthermore, the Mission will engage with international organizations engaged in Syria’s political transition process, with a view to ensuring coordination and complementarity.

With regard to intra-UN coordination, the Mission will maintain close coordination with the Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator, the UN country team, relevant UN humanitarian, development, and peacebuilding entities, mindful of the need to ensure a coherent “One UN” approach, maximize practical impact, avoid inefficiencies and duplication, and ensure that the partnership delivers tangible results for the Syrian people. The Mission will also support the International Independent Commission of Inquiry; the International, Impartial and Independent Mechanism; and the Independent Institution on Missing Persons. The Mission will focus on substantive areas where it can add distinct value in support of Syria’s political transition, guided by operational effectiveness.

The Mission will continue to integrate gender, disability, and anti-racism perspectives across its activities, including by renewing its gender strategy for 2026–2027 and adapting it to the new political context, promoting the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy through staff training and communications, and advancing the strategic action plan on racism and the promotion of dignity for all in the UN Secretariat, in coordination with the Anti-Racism Office.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 initiative –

The proposed programme plan for 2027 contains no significant change arising from the UN80 initiative and reflects efforts of the mission to implement all mandates in a more efficient and effective manner.
Evaluation activities

In 2025, the Office of Internal Oversight Services (OIOS) completed an evaluation on Cluster I conflict-specific Special Political Missions, OIOS found that the Mission was one successful example of effectively developing and implementing mechanisms for broadening inclusion of civil society and women. The Mission continues to implement successful methods for enhanced inclusion into its activities and programme plans.

In 2027, the Mission will regularly conduct internal evaluations of the efficiency and effectiveness of its activities, adjusting them as needed in response to evolving political dynamics or emerging needs and requests from the Syrian government and other partners. The results of these evaluations, including lessons learned, will inform future planning processes and be reflected in subsequent programme plans.
Programme performance in 2025
Constructive, coherent and comprehensive multilateral approach and continuous progress towards an inclusive, sustainable political solution in line with Security Council resolution 2254 (2015)

In 2025, the Special Envoy engaged with the caretaker authorities and the subsequently formed government, as well as the leadership of the Syrian Democratic Forces, leaders from the Druze, Alawite, Christian and other communities, a broad spectrum of Syrian civil society, and key regional and international partners, including through participation in international gatherings. Through these engagements, the Special Envoy helped maintain focus on a balanced, rights-based approach, emphasizing de-escalation, accountability, humanitarian access, reconstruction, detainees, and reconciliation, while promoting confidence-building and dialogue to address local concerns and safeguard Syria’s unity.

Overall, the Mission moved from a context of stalled mediation to active good offices engagement, advice and support. The value of this role lay in sustaining dialogue, promoting inclusivity, and aligning international efforts behind a Syrian-led and Syrian-owned political transition in line with the core elements of Security Council resolution 2254 (2015). At a critical juncture, this work helped preserve momentum and reinforced the principle that only negotiation, compromise, and broad participation - rather than rushed or exclusionary processes - can secure a durable and peaceful future for Syria. Steps so far on the institutional, constitutional, and governance front have been taken, and further progress is needed to ensure a fully inclusive and participatory transition.

Progress towards institutional consolidation and reform in line with the principles of Security Council resolution 2254 (2015), supported by the widest possible spectrum of Syrian stakeholders and underpinned by strong international consensus – Programme performance in 2025 and target for 2027

In 2025, the Mission’s work contributed to maintaining momentum around a Syrian-led and Syrian-owned political transition process, with improved alignment of national and international efforts in support of that process. It reinforced the principle that only dialogue, de-escalation, compromise, and broad participation can secure a durable and peaceful future for Syria. Despite these efforts, the planned targets for 2025 were not fully achieved, largely due to structural constraints and evolving realities on the ground.

In 2027, the Mission will continue to offer its good offices to advance a peaceful, orderly, transparent, and inclusive political transition, consistent with the principles of resolution 2254 (2015). The Mission seeks to become a trusted partner for the Syrian government and establish more systematic consultation and partnership, while also ensuring continued engagement with all other constituencies across the country.
Lessons learned and planned change

A key lesson for the Mission was the need to strengthen engagement on the ground and enhance accessibility to the Syrian government and the people it serves, in order to ensure closer alignment with evolving needs and realities and to better support the political transition process. In this regard, the potential establishment of small sub-offices in existing UN hubs outside Damascus, with the agreement of the Syrian government, will be evaluated as a means to improve operational outreach and deepen local engagement.

7.	Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for the Horn of Africa
A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

The mandate of the mission derives from an exchange of letters between the Secretary-General and the President of the Security Council (S/2018/955 and S/2018/979), when the remit of the mandate of the former Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for the Sudan and South Sudan was expanded to cover the entire Horn of Africa region, following previous exchanges of letters (including S/2016/258 and S/2016/259). In line with the letters of 2018, the mission also continues to carry out the functions previously performed by the Special Envoy for the Sudan and South Sudan relating to the maintenance of good and peaceful neighbourly relations between the Sudan and South Sudan, established pursuant to the exchange of letters between the Secretary-General and the President of the Security Council in 2011 (S/2011/474 and S/2011/475). The mandate includes cooperation with the African Union (AU) High-level Implementation Panel in efforts to implement Security Council resolution 2046 (2012), in which the Council called upon the Sudan and South Sudan to reach an agreement on critical issues, including: (a) the full and urgent advancement of all outstanding issues from the Comprehensive Peace Agreement; and (b) the easing of tensions and the facilitation of the resumption of negotiations on post-secession relations and the normalization of their relations. Furthermore, the mission works closely with and supports member States of the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), in line with the Joint Framework for Cooperation between the United Nations and IGAD signed in Djibouti on 17 November 2015, and other regional organizations in promoting peace and security across the Horn of Africa.
Programme of work
Objective

The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to establish and maintain good and peaceful neighbourly relations between the countries of the Horn of Africa region, encompassing Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Kenya, Somalia, South Sudan, the Sudan and Uganda, to consolidate and sustain gains in peace and security and enhance regional conflict prevention.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, the mission will:

Support regional peace and security, development, integration and inclusive governance, while addressing climate-security linkages, in line with the Pact for the Future. The mission will provide UN political leadership under the 2024-2028 Regional Prevention and Integration Strategy for the Horn of Africa (Regional Strategy), including preventive action on emerging conflicts. Strengthen cooperation with IGAD, the AU and partners to harmonize approaches through multilateral mechanisms;

Foster trust among member States and regional institutions through dialogue on divisive issues and encourage cooperation on climate adaptation, food security, infrastructure, Women Peace and Security (WPS) and Youth, Peace and Security (YPS) Agendas. The mission will leverage existing platforms, including the Friends of the Horn of Africa group and Horn of Africa Ambassadors, to promote constructive dialogues;

Utilize the Secretary-General’s good offices and the collective influence of IGAD member States to encourage dialogue and joint initiatives, including with middle‑powers, while harmonising efforts among international partner;

Collaborate with IGAD, the AU and other partners in addressing security threats through improved information-sharing, partner coordination and coherent messaging. The mission will undertake preventive engagement on political transitions and elections with regional implications, including South Sudan in February 2027 and in contexts affected by the reconfiguration of UN presences. The mission will leverage the UN’s convening authority to complement AU and IGAD‑led initiatives;

Support efforts to advance WPS and YPS in political dialogue and peace processes, including encouraging meaningful participation of women and youth and promoting inclusive approaches to conflict prevention and peacebuilding.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:

Enhanced subregional capacities, improved trust among member States, stronger dialogue on cross‑border and strategic issues, reduced tension and increased cooperation on shared challenges affecting regional stability;
Greater alignment of regional and international partners with UN, IGAD and AU strategic frameworks, advancing more coordinated regional approaches;

A more coherent One-UN approach in the region that supports the implementation of the Regional Strategy and integrates WPS, climate‑related risks and youth participation across peace and security, development and human rights work.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:

IGAD and the AU remain fully engaged in regional peace and security, maintaining focus on Ethiopia, Eritrea, Somalia, the Sudan and South Sudan, and advancing approaches that integrate gender, climate‑related and youth dimensions;
Regional states continue constructive engagement with the Special Envoy and the UN on capacity-building, particularly in mediation, conflict prevention and conflict resolution;

South Sudanese parties, with regional support, remain committed to implementing the Revitalized Agreement and ensuring a peaceful conclusion of the transitional period ending in February 2027, if not further extended;
Sudan - South Sudan relations remain constructive despite the war in the Sudan, allowing continued engagement on outstanding bilateral issues, including Abyei;
Relations among countries experiencing tensions continue on a path of de-escalation, allowing space for constructive dialogue;

Regional and national stakeholders remain committed to advancing WPS and YPS agendas, ensuring political space for meaningful participation of women and youth in political and peacebuilding processes.

With regard to cooperation with other entities, the mission works closely with IGAD and its member States, the AU, the European Union and other partners to address regional dimensions of crises, focusing on cross-border implications and supporting political cooperation and regional integration.

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the mission will continue its close engagement with the Personal Envoy of the Secretary-General for the Sudan, the Special Representative of the Secretary-General to the African Union, the Special Representative and Head of the United Nations Mission in South Sudan, Resident Coordinators, Peace and Development Advisers and UN entities across the Horn of Africa region to ensure a coherent approach to prevention. In 2027, this coordination will strengthen information-sharing and joint analysis, while reducing duplication to enable a more efficient and targeted use of resources.

The mission integrates a gender perspective across its operational activities, including good offices, missions, seminars and workshops. It promotes inclusive messaging and strengthens women’s participation in political and peace processes through engagement in regional and global WPS forums.

In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the mission will support IGAD and the AU in enhancing the participation of persons with disabilities in political, peace and security initiatives.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 initiative

The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects efforts of the mission to implement all mandates in a more efficient and effective manner and contains no substantive adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative.
Programme performance in 2025
Strengthened regional coherence and coordinated preventive action in the Horn of Africa

In 2025, the mission played a central role in advancing preventive diplomacy and confidence‑building amid regional tensions. Through sustained political engagement, the Special Envoy worked with regional leaders, neighbouring States and partners to promote dialogue. A key achievement was the establishment of structured engagement platforms, including the Friends of the Horn of Africa forum, which brings together permanent members of the Security Council and influential regional actors to align messaging and reduce fragmentation among external initiatives.

The mission also strengthened regional UN coordination through joint regional analysis, shared risk assessments, prioritizing collective action, leading to more effective information‑sharing, consistent messaging and better sequencing of diplomatic interventions in contexts marked by political transitions and protracted crises.

8.	Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for the Great Lakes Region
A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

The mandate of the mission derives from Security Council resolution 2098 (2013) and various subsequent Council resolutions, the latest being resolution 2808 (2025). Established in 2013, the mission is responsible for supporting the implementation of the Peace, Security and Cooperation Framework for the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Region, which was signed on 24 February 2013 by Angola, Burundi, the Central African Republic, the Congo, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Rwanda, South Africa, South Sudan, Uganda, the United Republic of Tanzania and Zambia, as well as representatives of the United Nations, the African Union, the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region and the Southern African Development Community, acting as guarantor institutions. On 31 January 2014, Kenya and the Sudan also signed the Framework. The Framework outlines national, regional and international commitments required to end the recurring cycles of violence in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and address the root causes of conflict in the region.

In its resolution 2808 (2025), the Security Council reaffirmed the importance of an integrated regional approach under the African Union and stressed the commitments undertaken by the signatories of the Peace, Security and Cooperation Framework not to tolerate nor provide assistance or support of any kind to armed groups.  In resolutions 2765 (2024), 2773 (2025) and 2808 (2025), the Council called on the Special Envoy to intensify his engagement to support the full implementation of the Framework, as well as to support regional peace processes and strengthen regional diplomatic mediation efforts.
Programme of work
Objective

The objective is to advance the effective implementation of the Peace, Security and Cooperation Framework by supporting and facilitating political, security and economic engagements between the signatory countries, while ensuring coherent and coordinated support from regional and international partners, in line with the United Nations Strategy for Peace Consolidation, Conflict Prevention and Conflict Resolution in the Great Lakes Region and its action Plan.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, the mission will:
Support signatory countries in efforts to implement the revitalized Peace, Security and Cooperation Framework;
Provide the Secretary-General’s good offices and enhance support to regional peace processes, including through assistance to mediation efforts and the implementation of agreements;

Support the implementation of regional non-military approaches to disarming, demobilizing, repatriating where applicable, and reintegrating members of armed groups, and help to strengthen existing security cooperation mechanisms;
Support the effective participation of civil society, women and youth in political and peacebuilding processes, and promote the economic empowerment of youth;
Promote regional economic integration, including the implementation of the recommendations of the high-level regional workshop on natural resources held in 2021 in Khartoum, Sudan;
Promote regional judicial cooperation, in close cooperation with the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR);

Support the implementation of the United Nations regional strategy and its Action Plan for the period 2025-2027, through coordination and provision of secretariat support to its Senior Policy Group and Implementation Support Mechanism.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:
Signatory countries of the Peace, Security and Cooperation Framework implementing recommendations from the revitalization process to address root causes of conflict;

Signatory countries engaging in regional peace processes and implementing political agreements, contributing to the de-escalation of bilateral tensions and improving the security and humanitarian situation in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo;

Countries concerned enhancing cooperation to address the threat posed by armed groups and coordinating regional disarmament, demobilization, repatriation and reintegration initiatives through the Contact and Coordination Group on non-military measures and its operational cell;
An increased number of civil society organizations, including women and youth, contributing to regional peace processes and cross-border peacebuilding initiatives;
Signatory countries strengthening regional judicial cooperation through the Great Lakes Judicial Cooperation Network;
Signatory countries increasing economic cooperation and implementing initiatives to curb the illicit exploitation of, and trade in natural resources, with a focus on artisanal gold and coltan;
United Nations entities enhancing coordination and ensuring greater alignment between national strategic cooperation frameworks and the objectives of the United Nations regional strategy.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
Eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo will continue to face insecurity, while relations between some countries will remain tense despite diplomatic efforts;
The Washington and Doha processes and the African Union-led mediation will require continued support;
The African Union-led mediation will continue, requiring sustained support from the United Nations and regional and international partners;

Continued support will be required to strengthen the participation and contribution of women and youth in the implementation of peace agreements, advancement of peace processes, and community peacebuilding;
Signatory countries of the Peace, Security and Cooperation Framework will demonstrate renewed political will to implement their commitments;
International partners will continue to support efforts towards a political settlement of the conflict in the Great Lakes region.

With regard to cooperation with other entities, the mission will enhance coordination with ICGLR to support complementary approaches under the Peace, Security and Cooperation Framework and the ICGLR Pact on Security, Stability and Development in the Great Lakes Region. The Special Envoy will continue to participate in the International Contact Group.

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the mission will continue to work closely with the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO), including on political and technical support to the ongoing peace processes, as well as in the context of regional cooperation on non-military measures related to disarmament, demobilization, repatriation and reintegration. Support to regional peace efforts will continue to be coordinated through a mechanism comprising the mission, MONUSCO, the United Nations Regional Office for Central Africa and the United Nations Office to the African Union.
