9.	Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Yemen
A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

The mission is responsible for exercising the good offices of the Secretary-General to enable the resumption of a peaceful, inclusive, orderly, Yemeni-led and Yemeni-owned political transition process that meets the legitimate demands and aspirations of the Yemeni people, including women and youth, for peaceful change and meaningful reform, as set out in the Initiative of the Gulf Cooperation Council and its implementation mechanism and the outcomes of the comprehensive National Dialogue Conference. The mandate derives from Security Council resolution 2014 (2011) and from subsequent Council resolutions, the latest being resolution 2813 (2026).

To ensure the implementation of Security Council resolutions 2014 (2011) and 2051 (2012), together with the political transition agreed in November 2011 under the Initiative of the Gulf Cooperation Council and its implementation mechanism for the political transition process in Yemen, the Secretary-General established the Office of the Special Adviser to the Secretary-General on Yemen, in accordance with an exchange of letters with the President of the Security Council in June 2012, which was then subsumed into the Office of the Special Envoy (S/2012/469 and S/2012/470).

In line with Council resolution 2216 (2015), as well as other Council resolutions on Yemen, including resolutions 2014 (2011), 2051 (2012), 2140 (2014), 2201 (2015), 2451 (2018), 2452 (2019), 2722 (2024) 2742 (2024) and 2813 (2026), and the letter from the Secretary-General addressed to the President of the Security Council (S/2016/488), the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Yemen will continue to mediate between the parties. While supporting the parties to implement the relevant aspects of the  Stockholm Agreement and its related Hudaydah Agreement (S/2018/1134, annex) as part of efforts towards reaching a Yemen-wide ceasefire, and to engage other Yemenis and regional and international stakeholders in support of the Yemeni transition process, and an inclusive Yemeni-led and Yemeni-owned political process under UN auspices.

Pursuant to Security Council resolution 2813 (2026), which terminated UNMHA’s mandate and transferred its residual tasks to the Office of the Special Envoy, the mission  will support the parties to implement the Agreement on the City of Hudaydah and the Ports of Hudaydah, Salif and Ra’s Isa (Hudaydah Agreement), as endorsed by the Security Council in its resolution 2451 (2018), as well as integrate these relevant tasks into its security-related engagement, including the convening of the Redeployment Coordination Committee, coordination of mine action activities, and monitoring and reporting on military and security developments, as well as periodic visits.
Programme of work
Objective

The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to achieve a negotiated political settlement between the parties to end the conflict in Yemen and enable the resumption of a peaceful, inclusive, orderly, Yemeni-led and Yemeni-owned political transition that will lead Yemenis towards a path of sustainable peace.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, the mission will:

Lead mediation efforts with the parties, supported by regional and international actors, to identify confidence-building measures and advance the political process. To ensure inclusive participation and the reflection of the priorities of the broader Yemeni population, the mission will regularly consult Yemeni political parties, women, youth, civil society and other stakeholders through inclusive consultation formats. The mission will mediate further releases of conflict-related detainees;

Engage the parties and security actors, including through the Military Coordination Committee as part of the efforts to reach a Yemen-wide ceasefire and agreements on longer term security arrangements. The mission will also chair the Redeployment Coordination Committee, monitor and report on relevant developments, and coordinate mine action to implement the residual tasks of the Hudaydah Agreement;

Mediate between the parties, while also engaging technical experts, the private sector, international financial institutions and other relevant stakeholders, to advance near-term economic de-escalation and confidence-building measures, as well as to identify solutions to longer-term economic issues essential to a comprehensive resolution to the conflict;

Continue to support the parties to implement the Hudaydah Agreement through the collection and collation of information pertaining to the implementation of the Agreement, chairing of the Redeployment Coordination Committee in order to achieve and sustain de-escalation, supporting measures to mitigate security risks affecting civilians and civilian movement, advancement of mine action interventions, and further releases of conflict-related detainees in furtherance of the broader UN-facilitated political process.
Engage with regional stakeholders, the UN Security Council, and the wider international community to maintain concerted diplomatic backing for the UN mediation process;

Utilize strategic communications to support the implementation of the mission’s mandate by strengthening public understanding of the UN-facilitated political process, enhancing transparency across the political, economic and security tracks, and fostering an informed information environment that mitigates misinformation and supports constructive engagement among Yemeni stakeholders.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:

Progress towards agreements between the parties on political, economic and military/security measures that improve living conditions in Yemen and contribute to a sustainable, peaceful and inclusive settlement of the conflict;
Engagement with diverse Yemeni political and social stakeholders, including women, youth, media entities and the broader public, to inform the UN-led mediation process;
Sustained, coherent international and regional support for the UN-led mediation process.

With regard to cooperation with other entities, the mission engages closely with international and regional organizations, including the League of Arab States, the Gulf Cooperation Council, the European Union and the International Committee of the Red Cross, and other international partners, including international financial institutions.

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the mission cooperates with the Resident/Humanitarian Coordinator and the United Nations country team in Yemen. The mission consults and coordinates closely with the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs and with other special political missions in the region.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:

The parties will continue to engage with the Office and, to the extent possible, facilitate access and conditions necessary to sustain dialogue, support de-escalation efforts and enable continued engagement with Yemeni stakeholders, amid a constrained and evolving operating environment;

Despite a complex mediation environment impacted by regional dynamics, ongoing conflict, and a constrained operating environment, international and Yemeni support for the UN-led mediation process is sustained;

The mission maintains its presence in Yemen in Sana’a and Aden and continues to have access to key Yemeni stakeholders, including through digital means, albeit with restrictions due to the security situation on the ground.

The mission continues to integrate a gender perspective into its operations, including by ensuring the meaningful inclusion of women in the mediation process and by ensuring their perspectives inform the negotiation agenda and outcomes.
In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the mission will ensure that its engagement approaches are inclusive of persons with disabilities.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 initiative

The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects efforts of the mission to implement all mandates in a more efficient and effective manner and contains no substantive adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative.
Evaluation activities

In 2025, the Office of Internal Oversight Services (OIOS), as indicated in paragraph 10 in this report, completed an evaluation of conflict specific special political missions under thematic cluster I which have guided the proposed programme plan for 2027.

In response to this evaluation, the mission will strengthen the discipline and coherence of its internal planning, including clearer prioritization and closer integration across its political, economic and security tracks, and will make more systematic use of existing mechanisms for information-sharing and internal coordination across its duty stations, while continuing to apply remote modalities, as reflected in its strategy, to sustain consultations and outreach in a constrained operating environment.
Programme performance in 2025
The multitrack UN-led mediation process advanced

In 2025, the mission advanced efforts in support of the United Nations-facilitated political process. On the political track, the mission regularly engaged with the conflict parties, as well as regional and international actors. The mission also held political consultations with diverse Yemeni political actors, women, media, youth and civil society across multiple governorates. Despite tensions in the region, the Red Sea, and parts of southern Yemen, front lines within Yemen remained broadly stable, with the mission’s proactive and broad engagement contributing to preserving space for continued dialogue. The mission also co-convened, with the International Committee of the Red Cross, a meeting of the Supervisory Committee on the implementation of the detainees’ agreement in Muscat, which resulted in an initial agreement that marked a step forward for the potential release of thousands of conflict-related detainees.

On the economic track, the mission engaged with senior Government of Yemen and Houthi-affiliated officials, as well as with key and senior private sector actors to better understand key economic developments, issues and pressure points impacting the conflict; and to identify viable entry points, with a focus on confidence-building measures and developing concrete solutions, for example, overcoming the bifurcation of the Central Bank and the currency. On the military/security track, the mission convened six meetings with delegations of the Military Coordination Committee to discuss and plan for a national ceasefire and transitional security arrangements.

In 2027, the mission will continue efforts on sustaining and further broadening inclusive engagement with Yemeni stakeholders across political, economic and security tracks, including through the mission’s presence in Yemen (Aden and Sana’a) and Jordan, as well as through periodic missions to Hudaydah Governorate and elsewhere, and engagement at local, national and regional levels.

Result 2: increased clarity and shared understanding among interlocutors on priority de-escalatory, confidence-building and economic proposals contributing to improved living conditions for Yemenis – Programme performance in 2025 and target for 2027

In 2025, the mission engaged interlocutors across political, military-security and economic tracks, including through expert consultations on economic issues, engagement on conflict-related detainees and support for local confidence-building measures such as the reopening of key roads, contributing to maintaining relative stability and supporting civilian movement and economic activity. Building on this, in 2027, the mission will continue to engage on priority proposals across tracks, with a view to supporting more informed consideration of such measures.
Lessons learned and planned change

The lesson for the mission was that engagement on increasingly technical and complex proposals requires not only sustained dialogue, but also a sufficient level of shared understanding among interlocutors to support informed consideration and avoid misinterpretation. In applying the lesson, the mission will place greater emphasis on iterative and inclusive engagement on priority proposals across political, military-security and economic tracks, supported by more structured analytical input and coordinated complementary channels, including Track II engagement and other coordinated efforts, to support more informed and coherent consideration of such proposals.

10.	Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General on Myanmar
A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

The mission is responsible for the provision of the Secretary-General’s good offices through discussions involving all relevant stakeholders and assistance to Myanmar. The mandate was defined by the General Assembly in its resolution 72/248 and has been renewed on a yearly basis since, most recently in resolution 80/221. In resolution 2669 (2022), the Security Council reinforced the urgent need to end the human suffering, and provided further guidance on the scope of work of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General, including by encouraging close coordination with the Special Envoy of the ASEAN Chair on Myanmar. The situation in Myanmar continues to deteriorate following the military takeover of February 2021, with serious regional impacts and implications for the human rights of the Rohingya Muslims and other groups. Fighting between the Myanmar armed forces and ethnic armed organizations and other resistance forces has continued to intensify and has severely affected civilians.
Programme of work
Objective

The objective, to which the mission contributes, is to support an inclusive Myanmar-led democratic and peaceful nation-building process and the creation of conditions that are conducive to the voluntary, safe, dignified and sustainable return and reintegration of Rohingya in Myanmar.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective and address the deteriorating situation in Myanmar, the mission will:

Implement a multitrack approach, in accordance with the Pact for the Future, including strengthening cooperation between the United Nations and ASEAN. In close coordination with the Special Envoy of the ASEAN Chair and United Nations partners, the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General will seek to support Myanmar-led processes for the resolution of the crisis. The Special Envoy will complement regional efforts to support the effective implementation of the ASEAN five-point consensus, aligned with the needs of the people of Myanmar, and will support the coordinated humanitarian and development engagement of the United Nations system;

Advocate for a Myanmar-led process towards a peaceful, democratic and inclusive future and promote a coherent international and regional approach. The mission will continue to initiate inclusive and participatory approaches with minorities, youth and women, whose voices are critical to fostering social cohesion and developing a way out of the current political crisis in line with the will of the people;

Continue efforts to create an environment that is conducive to the voluntary, safe, dignified and sustainable return to Rakhine State of the forcibly displaced Rohingya in the region, including from Bangladesh. The Special Envoy will continue to promote a political solution that addresses the underlying issues in consultation with the Rohingya, and to advocate for the improvement of the conditions on the ground, in line with the recommendations of the Advisory Commission on Rakhine State and the commitments made at the General Assembly High-level Conference on the Situation of Rohingya Muslims and Other Minorities in Myanmar, held on 30 September 2025.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:
Improved conditions for the safe, voluntary, dignified and sustainable return of forcibly displaced populations;
The creation of conditions that are conducive to a de-escalation of violence and an increase in trust among communities;
Greater international and regional political support towards Myanmar-led processes for the resolution of the crisis;

Key stakeholders advancing discussions towards the establishment of a Myanmar-led process on restoring democratic and human rights norms, and continued engagement with all stakeholders to identify potential for common ground.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:

A viable path back to civilian rule is grounded on cessation of violence and a genuine commitment to inclusive dialogue with the full participation of civil society, including women, youth, ethnic and minority communities;

The impact on civilians from the continued violence since the military takeover, serious human rights violations and the need for civilian protection will remain a significant challenge in restoring peace in the country;

The situation will continue to require concrete actions towards improved conditions to allow for the safe, dignified, voluntary and sustainable return of the Rohingya and their reintegration in Myanmar. The rights and security of the Rohingya people need to be guaranteed and embedded in Myanmar-led solutions towards a peaceful, democratic and inclusive future;

Illicit activities and related financial flows, closely linked to the conflict in Myanmar and the downfall of the formal economy, will continue to hamper conflict resolution and impede socioeconomic and development efforts. Expansion of transnational crime networks emanating from Myanmar will have increasing regional implications.

With regard to cooperation with other entities, the mission works in partnership with ASEAN, especially the Special Envoy of the ASEAN Chair, other key regional organizations, such as the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) and the European Union, neighbouring countries and international donors to mobilize support to Myanmar-led processes for the resolution of the crisis.

The mission coordinates closely with the United Nations system through established channels, in close consultation with the Resident Coordinators in Myanmar and Bangladesh. The Special Envoy of the Secretary-General continues to carry out the good offices mandate in close cooperation with the United Nations country team, regional offices and Headquarters, as well as mechanisms on Myanmar mandated by the Human Rights Council. The mission also works in partnership with United Nations entities to foster inclusion of diverse and vulnerable groups, such as women and youth, in dialogue processes.

The mission integrates gender perspectives into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate, and supports efforts to strengthen the capacity of Myanmar women to participate regionally and globally in women and peace and security engagements and to amplify the voices of the most marginalized women.
In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the mission will foster the inclusion of persons with disabilities in its political strategy and its efforts on building inclusion.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 initiative

The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects changes arising from the UN80 Initiative. In particular, the tables of deliverables reflect updated planned deliverables for 2026, in line with the approved programme budget for 2026.
Programme performance in 2025
Cessation of violence and progress toward a Myanmar-led political solution to the crisis, including creating conditions conducive to the return of refugees

In 2025, the Special Envoy engaged Myanmar stakeholders, Member States and civil society to explore pathways toward a Myanmar-led political solution to the country’s multidimensional crisis and its regional implications. During her visits to Myanmar, the Special Envoy underscored the opportunity for the country to unite in response to the March 2025 earthquakes and for building momentum toward a cessation of hostilities and an inclusive political process. While several armed actors declared unilateral ceasefires to allow for rescue and recovery efforts, these were ultimately not sustained, and violence continued. Through continuous engagement, including participation in the General Assembly High-level Conference on the Situation of Rohingya Muslims and other Minorities in Myanmar, the Special Envoy helped renew international attention to the Rohingya crisis and generate new funding pledges for the response. Strong coordination with the ASEAN Special Envoy and advancing UN-ASEAN cooperation, including joint women, peace and security initiatives, helped amplify the voices of Myanmar women. The Special Envoy also continued efforts to promote system-wide coherence, and safeguard the operating space of the United Nations country team in Myanmar.

11.	Office of the Personal Envoy of the Secretary-General for the Sudan
A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

The mandate of the Office of the Personal Envoy of the Secretary-General for the Sudan derives from Security Council resolution 2715 (2023), in which the Council, expressing alarm at the continued violence and humanitarian situation, in particular violations of international humanitarian law and grave human rights violations and abuses, welcomed the appointment of the Personal Envoy to use his good offices with the parties and the neighbouring States, complementing regional peace efforts, including those of the African Union and IGAD, and called on all parties to extend their cooperation in furtherance of his tasks. This was reiterated by the Council in its resolution 2724 (2024), in which it encouraged the Personal Envoy to use his good offices with the parties and the neighbouring States, complementing and coordinating regional peace efforts. In its resolution 2736 (2024), the Council called on the parties to the conflict to seek an immediate cessation of hostilities, leading to a sustainable resolution to the conflict, through dialogue, with the continued support of the Personal Envoy and the African Union High-level Implementation Panel. The Council encouraged the coordinated engagement of the Personal Envoy with the African Union, LAS and other key regional actors, to help to advance peace and an inclusive and comprehensive Sudanese-led political process, with the full, equal, meaningful and safe participation of women, that reflected the aspirations of the Sudanese people.
Programme of work
Objective

The objective to which this mission contributes, is to seek an immediate cessation of hostilities, leading to a sustainable resolution to the Sudan conflict, and to advance a lasting peace through dialogue and an inclusive and comprehensive Sudanese-led political process that reflects the aspirations of the Sudanese people.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, the mission will:

Through good offices, consultations and shuttle diplomacy, support dialogue between the parties towards a cessation of hostilities, enhanced protection of civilians and the launch of an inclusive Sudanese-led political process, with the full, equal, meaningful and safe participation of women, in close collaboration with national, regional and international stakeholders;

Support efforts aimed at reaching and implementing temporary truces and sequenced steps toward a cessation of hostilities, including confidence-building measures, in coordination with relevant regional and international actors;

Support the coordination of international mediation initiatives by bringing together key regional and international stakeholders to enhance the overall effectiveness, coherence and integration of these initiatives and maximize their comparative advantages. Efforts will be aimed at harmonizing tracks of multilateral engagement, maximizing impact and leveraging peacemaking efforts, and advancing strategies on ensuring an inclusive process;
Foster continued regional and international support for resolving the conflict in the Sudan, notably through advocacy, frequent dialogue and information exchange;

Sustain and support consultations with a broad range of Sudanese civilian forces, including women and youth, to contribute to the United Nations initiatives aimed at advancing a cessation of hostilities, improving civilian protection in the Sudan and supporting an inclusive Sudanese-led political process.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:

Parties making progress towards a negotiated cessation of hostilities, including through localized or issue-specific agreements, including those relating to transitional security arrangements, the protection of civilians and the advancement of humanitarian access;

Technical coordination mechanisms in place to effectively enable efforts to reach and implement negotiated humanitarian truces and cessation of hostilities agreements -including through clear roles and responsibilities, communication mechanisms, and reporting structures;

Peace efforts being well coordinated, with clarity on the roles and respective responsibilities of stakeholders, on the basis of comparative advantage and taking account of capacities, leverage and any prior engagement on the issues, while giving effect to the principle of partnership and ensuring effective coordination of facilitation and other engagements;
Possible outcomes of the peace and political processes being agreed through established mediation or facilitation frameworks;
Civilian stakeholders being effectively engaged and informed on United Nations peacebuilding and peacemaking initiatives.

With regard to cooperation and coordination with other entities, the mission will liaise closely with all international and regional stakeholders involved in support of peace efforts in the Sudan, in particular the African Union, IGAD, LAS, and the European Union as well as neighbouring States. In doing so, it will work through established regional and Member State mechanisms to deepen strategic and operational engagements in carrying out good offices and mediation. It will also liaise closely with civilian actors through the various established civilian peacemaking platforms.

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the mission will cooperate with the Resident Coordinator/Humanitarian Coordinator and the agencies, funds and programmes of the United Nations operating in the Sudan and the region, and coordinate closely with the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs and special political missions and peacekeeping operations in the region
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:

The situation in the Sudan is likely to remain highly volatile, with the possibility of further fragmentation of political dynamics and increased hostilities. While a nationwide agreement on a cessation of hostilities may take time, there could be temporary, localized ceasefires;

Shifting regional and international dynamics may create intermittent openings for de-escalation or renewed political engagement, including limited humanitarian truces or other focused measures creating space to alleviate civilian suffering and build incremental confidence between the parties in view of a permanent ceasefire;

The international community will remain actively engaged in support of peace efforts in the Sudan, and the parties to the conflict will continue to engage in discussions with the Personal Envoy to advance a Sudanese-led political process.

The mission integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate. This includes promoting the full, equal, meaningful and safe participation of women in political and mediation processes and by ensuring that gender consideration inform analysis, engagement and reporting. The mission supports activities to advance gender-related issues and provides support for greater civic engagement towards more inclusive peace and political processes. The mission prioritizes regular consultations with Sudanese women to solicit their insights, views on developments in Sudan, and perspectives on the protection of civilians, particularly women, equal access to humanitarian aid and other concerns pertaining to participation in peace processes. This inclusive approach will allow Sudanese women to voice their concerns, needs and experiences.

In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the mission will seek to promote disability inclusion internally by creating space for employment opportunities for qualified candidates. At the political level, it will advocate for inclusion of the views of persons with disabilities in decision-making platforms, as change agents for peace, security and sustainable development.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 initiative

The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects changes arising from the UN80 Initiative. In particular, the tables of deliverables reflect updated planned deliverables for 2026, in line with the approved programme budget for 2026.
Programme performance in 2025
De-escalation and an inclusive political process

In 2025, against an increasingly fragmented and volatile political environment marked by continued hostilities, heightened risks to civilians and competing political trajectories, the Office of the Personal Envoy intensified its good offices with the conflict parties to maintain direct engagement, incentivizing dialogue and de-escalation, maintaining channels active with the parties, and raising attention on the violence and its impact on the civilians. Extensive consultations took place between the Office and Sudanese civilian and political actors across the spectrum, including women and youth, underscoring a shared demand for an immediate ceasefire, interim measures to protect civilians and a civilian-led transition anchored in an inclusive Sudanese owned political process.

In parallel, the Office played a facilitating role in strengthening coordination among mediation actors. These efforts resulted in enhanced common messaging, further clarity on partners’ roles and greater complementarity of effort. The Office also began preparatory work to strengthen the political track, including comparative analysis of political visions and road maps articulated by Sudanese stakeholders, to contribute to shared understanding and preparedness for structured consultations in support of an inclusive Sudanese owned political process.

The mission supported the Consultative Meetings on Enhancing Coordination of Peace Initiatives, including the fourth meeting in June 2025, facilitated the operationalisation of a technical-level Task Force in January 2025, and reinforced multilateral coordination through the consolidation of the Quintet framework. Lessons learned and planned change

The mission’s experience in 2025 confirmed that stronger coordination at multiple levels is one of the Mission’s most effective tools to reduce fragmentation, discourage disparate peace efforts, and promote convergence around a coherent political process. In applying these lessons, the mission will prioritize structured coordination through established mechanisms, including the Consultative Meetings and the Quintet framework, and focus on sequenced consultations, supported by analytical and preparatory work, while expanding the use of virtual and hybrid modalities to sustain inclusive participation.

12.	Senior Representative for the implementation of Security Council resolution 2792 (2025)
A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 – Overall orientation – Mandates and background

The Security Council, in its resolution 2792 (2025), recalled its relevant resolutions on the ongoing cooperation between Iraq and Kuwait on the return of Kuwaiti property and the national archives and the repatriation or return of all Kuwaiti and third-country nationals or their remains (“missing persons and property”), in particular resolutions 2107 (2013) and 2732 (2024), and underlined the humanitarian nature of those efforts. In its resolution 2792 (2025), the Council requested the Secretary-General to appoint a senior representative whose mandate would focus solely on promoting, supporting and facilitating efforts regarding the repatriation or return of all Kuwaiti and third-country nationals or their remains and the return of Kuwaiti property, including the national archives.

The mandate of the Senior Representative derives from Security Council resolution 2792 (2025), in which the Council requested the Secretary-General to keep it informed every six months and to make available his good offices to strengthen confidence and mutual trust between Iraq and Kuwait on missing persons and property. The Council encouraged continued efforts, with the support of the Senior Representative and the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), including through excavation of all sites of interest and making use of technology advances. The Council encouraged Member States to provide access and additional funding and training for, among others, forensic sciences, DNA analysis, satellite maps and imagery, and ground-penetrating radar. It welcomed capacity-building on innovative technologies and the sharing of lessons learned, for example, the training workshop for technical experts and decision makers conducted in Nicosia by the Committee on Missing Persons in Cyprus in 2024. The Council underlined that it would consider the continued need for United Nations oversight of missing persons and property no later than 31 December 2030, or sooner in the event of sufficient progress, and expressed its intention to review the situation by 30 June 2028.
Programme of work – Objective

The objective, to which the Senior Representative contributes, is the repatriation or return of all Kuwaiti and third-country nationals or their remains and the return of Kuwaiti property, including the national archives, as well as fostering confidence and mutual trust between Iraq and Kuwait on missing persons and property.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, the Senior Representative will:

(a)	Promote, support and facilitate efforts regarding the repatriation or return of missing Kuwaiti and third-country nationals, or their remains, and the return of Kuwaiti property, including the national archives;
(b)	Exercise the good offices of the Secretary-General to facilitate dialogue, build trust and overcome political or technical obstacles to the implementation of the mandate;
(c)	Advocate for sustained political commitment from national authorities and international partners and promote coordination and information-sharing between Iraqi and Kuwaiti institutions;
(d)	Encourage the use of modern technologies and methodologies, such as DNA analysis, satellite imagery and archival research;
(e)	Encourage the strengthening of technical capacity through training and knowledge transfer on modern technologies.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:
(a)	Expedited repatriation of the remains of Kuwaiti and third-country nationals and the accelerated return of Kuwaiti property, including the national archives;

(b)	Building of mutual trust and enhanced cooperation between Iraq and Kuwait to foster confidence and sustain engagement and the political will to make progress in the search for missing Kuwaiti and third-country nationals and the return of missing Kuwaiti property, including the national archives;
(c)	Increased efficacy of search and identification efforts.

With regard to cooperation and coordination with other entities at the global, regional, national and local levels, the Senior Representative will liaise closely with all international and regional stakeholders involved in support of the implementation of the mandate, in particular the Iraqi authorities, including the Ministry of Defence, Kuwaiti authorities the members of the Tripartite Commission, namely, France, Saudi Arabia, the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland and the United States of America, and ICRC.

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Senior Representative will continue to operate in a collaborative way to ensure coherent and effective support for the implementation of Security Council resolution 2792 (2025). The Senior Representative is supported by the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs and will work closely with other United Nations entities, as appropriate.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a)	Iraqi and Kuwaiti authorities will continue to maintain constructive engagement with each other and with the Senior Representative;
(b)	Adequate financial resources, technical expertise and access to modern technologies will be secured to support search, identification and repatriation efforts;
(c)	Security conditions at burial sites of interest will remain sufficiently stable to allow safe access for field missions and technical teams.

The mission will integrate a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate in line with Security Council resolution 2792 (2025). The mission will encourage Iraqi and Kuwaiti counterparts to apply gender-responsive approaches in the search for missing persons, including in forensic processes and data collection.

In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the mission will seek to promote disability inclusion internally by creating space for employment opportunities for qualified candidates. At the political level, it will encourage, as appropriate, national authorities and relevant stakeholders to apply disability inclusive approaches in forensic and technological processes related to the search for missing persons and property.

Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions

Without prejudice to the distinct mandates of each entity, and subject to the decisions of the legislative bodies, as appropriate, the Advisory Committee trusts that the Secretary-General, in the context of the UN80 Initiative, will identify opportunities for consolidation of the United Nations presence, in particular where multiple entities coexist, and for further rationalization of functions and strengthened synergies among entities, including a clear delineation of roles to be performed by the missions and by the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs. The Committee looks forward to receiving relevant proposals in the next budget submission (para. 8)

Special Political Missions remain committed to strengthening the efficiency, coherence and effectiveness of the United Nations system while fully respecting the distinct mandates established by legislative bodies and the specific political, operational and security requirements of each mission.
In this regard, opportunities for consolidation of support structures, rationalization of administrative and back-office functions, and strengthened common services are being examined where feasible and without prejudice to mandate implementation. For special political missions, such efforts will continue to be pursued on a case-by-case basis, taking into account host-country conditions, mission size, security considerations and the need to preserve operational agility and political responsiveness. An example of this approach is the closure of the United Nations Mission to support the Hudaydah Agreement (UNMHA) and the transfer of related functions to the Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Yemen, a decision taken by the Security Council in January 2026 based on the options presented by the Secretary-General, with a view to streamlining the United Nations presence and ensuring continued support to the political process through more integrated arrangements.  
Special Political Missions also recognizes the importance of clearer delineation of responsibilities between missions and the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs, particularly in areas such as strategic guidance, policy support, programmatic backstopping and administrative service delivery. 
Any specific proposals with programmatic, structural or resource implications will be submitted for the consideration of Member States in future budget submissions, as appropriate.

The Advisory Committee has repeatedly emphasized the continued need to monitor the large number of high-level posts and avoid their proliferation across the Organization. The Committee therefore welcomes the proposal to abolish high-level posts within special political missions and the ongoing efforts under the UN80 Initiative to reduce duplication at the senior leadership level. The Committee trusts that the Secretary-General will continue to holistically assess mission structures, as well as the number and level of posts, to ensure balanced staffing components, including through rejuvenation and by maintaining and recruiting lower-level staff, and that related proposals will be presented in the next budget submission. (para. 9).

Cluster I missions take note of the observations of the Advisory Committee and reaffirm their commitment to maintaining staffing structures that are efficient, fit for purpose and aligned with evolving mandate requirements. In this regard, the missions remain committed to ensuring an appropriate balance in staffing components, including through careful management of the number and level of posts, efforts to reduce high-level posts where feasible, and measures to promote rejuvenation and increased nationalization of posts, while preserving the substantive and operational capacities required for effective mandate implementation.
At the same time, it is noted that Cluster I missions are generally small in size and operate with already lean structures. Further, Cluster I missions had already put forward reductions of high-level posts as part of the revised estimates submitted for the 2026 budget, including the abolishment of 7 posts (1 USG, 1 ASG, 5 P-5) and downward reclassification of two D-2 to D-1 posts. As a result, opportunities to further reduce senior-level posts are limited and must be considered carefully to avoid adversely affecting leadership capacity, political engagement, managerial oversight and delivery of mandated activities. Any adjustments to mission structures therefore require a case-by-case assessment based on operational realities and mandate needs.
Notwithstanding these constraints, Cluster I missions have continued to identify efficiencies and contribute to the broader objectives of the organization. Current proposals include the abolishment of an Under-Secretary-General level post in the Office of Support for the implementation of Security Council resolution 1559 (2004), as well as the proposal in the Office of the Special Envoy for Syria to reclassify downward one D-1 post to the P-5 level. These measures reflect continued efforts to streamline senior leadership structures and reduce duplication where appropriate.
Cluster I missions will continue to holistically review mission structures and staffing profiles, including the number and level of posts, with a view to ensuring balanced staffing components, supporting rejuvenation and sustaining mandate delivery. Any further proposals with structural or resource implications will be presented for the consideration of Member States in future budget submissions, as appropriate.

The Advisory Committee trusts that the Secretary-General will ensure the continued implementation of mandated activities and address challenges related to the proposed level of resources. The Committee looks forward to receiving updated information on mandate implementation and comprehensive mitigation plans in the next budget submission. (para. 10).

Cluster I Special Political Missions remain committed to the continued implementation of all mandated activities within the level of resources approved by the General Assembly. In the context of the UN80 Initiative and evolving resource parameters, Missions continue to prioritize the effective delivery of their mandate through targeted mitigation measures designed to preserve substantive impact while enhancing efficiency.
To mitigate the impact of resource constraints, Missions have sought efficiencies through strengthened collaboration and coordination with the established network of regional Resident Coordinators, relevant field operations and United Nations Country Teams, as well as with regional and subregional organizations. These efforts are intended to maximize complementarities, avoid duplication and leverage existing capacities across the wider United Nations system.
Missions have also expanded the use of technology to support mandate delivery, including increased recourse to virtual meetings, online collaboration platforms and digital training tools. These measures are expected to sustain outreach, engagement and knowledge-sharing in a cost-effective manner while improving operational flexibility.
In addition, the Missions continue to identify opportunities for cost optimization under operational expenditures, including through prudent management of travel, contractual services, facilities and other non-post resources, while safeguarding critical programmatic and security requirements.
Any adjustments to the programme plan arising from the UN80 initiative are presented as part of the current report under each mission.

Without prejudice to the separate mandate of the mission, pursuant to Security Council resolutions 1559 (2004) and 1680 (2006), the Advisory Committee trusts that the Secretary-General, in the context of the UN80 Initiative, will identify opportunities for further synergies among relevant entities operating in similar geographical or thematic areas, with relevant proposals to be presented in the next budget submission (para.42)

The position of Special Envoy for the Implementation of Security Council resolution 1559 (2004), at the level of Under-Secretary-General, will be abolished as part of efforts to enhance coherence and synergies in line with the UN80 Initiative. The functions previously exercised by the Special Envoy will be assumed by the Department of Peacebuilding and Political Affairs led by the Under-Secretary-General for Peacebuilding and Political Affairs, supported by dedicated capacity to implement the mandate. This consolidation is intended to strengthen overall UN leadership and coordination while avoiding duplication.

Noting the continuing suspension of the Gali Incident Prevention and Response Mechanism, the Advisory Committee is of the view that a comprehensive assessment of the actual requirements of the mission, including a fuller cost-benefit analysis of its locations vis-à-vis mandate implementation and the consideration of potential additional staffing adjustments, taking also into account existing capacity within the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs, should be presented in the next budget submission. (para. 46c).

UNRGID’s operational requirements are driven by its mandated responsibilities, including support to the Geneva International Discussions, participation in pre-round consultations with stakeholders, facilitation of the Incident Prevention and Response Mechanism, liaison with participants, coordination with humanitarian partners, and regular analysis and reporting to Headquarters.
Following approval of the revised estimates under the UN80 Initiative, strategic leadership and the functions of the UN Co-Chair of the Geneva International Discussions were transferred to the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs (DPPA) in New York effective January 2026. Accordingly, DPPA conducted a cost-benefit analysis of the redeployment of the P-3 post to New York to provide substantive support to the UN Co-Chair and strengthen coordination with EU and OSCE Co-Chairs at Headquarters level. The analysis indicates that the redeployment would generate estimated savings of approximately $6,800 through lower post adjustment costs compared with Geneva. In addition, the creation of one Administrative Assistant (GS-OL) post is considered necessary to provide administrative and operational support following the abolishment of the corresponding post in Geneva. These staffing changes are intended to ensure effective support for the Discussions and strengthened oversight and management of UNRGID.

Considering the existing capacity within the regional structure shared by the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs and the Department of Peace Operations, the Advisory Committee trusts that, in the context of the ongoing efforts under the UN80 Initiative, the requirement for the post of Senior Political Officer (P-5) in New York will be reassessed, with proposals to be included in the next budget submission. (para. 85).

The Senior Political Affairs Officer, based at Headquarters leads the Sudan team within the DPPA–DPO regional structure which serves as the liaison between the Office of the Personal Envoy of the Secretary-General on Sudan and Headquarters, with distinct responsibilities that include engagement with Security Council members and advising senior leadership. This requires a high level of experience and seniority and full-time engagement and could not be absorbed by existing teams covering other files. 
The Sudan team’s workload remains among the heaviest in the DPPA–DPO regional structure. Continued conflict escalation and intensified peacemaking efforts have driven a substantial increase in diplomatic activity on Sudan, including Security Council activity, requiring sustained Headquarters engagement. In this context, supporting the Personal Envoy of the Secretary-General for Sudan, who leads UN political engagement to help end the conflict, requires a dedicated Senior Political Affairs Officer to ensure coherence in the UN’s political engagement on Sudan. The post is also necessary to provide day-to-day leadership to the DPPA-DPO Sudan team, as well as strategic advice to senior UN officials, while ensuring effective coordination among UN entities at Headquarters. With the appointment of a new Personal Envoy in 2026, the activity of the Envoy’s office is expected to increase further, underscoring the need to preserve this critical Headquarters capacity.

In view of the resource optimization efforts under the UN80 Initiative, the Advisory Committee trusts that updated information on the complementarity of functions and coordination among entities addressing hate speech across the United Nations, along with an overview of dedicated resources across all funding sources, will be provided in future budget proposals. (para. 88)

The Office of the Special Adviser to the Secretary-General on the Prevention of Genocide is the United Nations system-wide focal point on hate speech and coordinates the implementation of the United Nations Strategy and Plan of Action on Hate Speech across the United Nations system. In this capacity, the Office coordinates and chairs the Working Group on Hate Speech, which comprises 19 United Nations entities that work on tackling hate speech from the perspective of their specific mandates. The Strategy and the Working Group enable the United Nations system to bring together its efforts under a common vision and strategic objectives, as outlined in the Strategy, and to ensure maximum impact across the United Nations system.

The Committee recalls that UNAMI previously carried out the functions pertaining to resolution 2792 (2025) from Iraq. The Advisory Committee considers that the proposed Headquarters location should be kept under review, based on the mission’s operational requirements, and trusts that updated information will be provided in the next budget submission, including consideration of its relocation closer to the area of operations, taking into account also efficiencies under official travel requirements. The Secretariat takes note of the Advisory Committee’s recommendation that the proposed Headquarters location should be kept under review in light of evolving operational requirements. In this regard, it may be recalled that, subsequent to the last budget submission, the Fifth Committee approved one P-4 Political Affairs Officer post but did not approve the requested General Service (GS) administrative support post.
Against this backdrop, the Secretariat considers that, at present, maintaining the duty station in New York reflects both the political and Security Council–focused nature of the mandate under resolution 2792 (2025) and the most efficient use of the limited resources available. Being based at Headquarters enables direct and routine access to the Security Council, the Executive Office of the Secretary-General and the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs (DPPA), which is essential for timely briefings, and consultations.
This configuration is further shaped by the current resource structure, whereby the Senior Representative is supported by a single P-4 Political Affairs Officer embedded within the Middle East Division of DPPA, with no dedicated administrative support post. The Senior Representative and the P-4 therefore rely extensively on existing capacities within the Middle East Division for a wide range of administrative and logistical support functions, including the scheduling of meetings, travel arrangements, visa processing and other related requirements. Maintaining the duty station in New York allows the mechanism to fully leverage these existing support structures, enabling a very small team to operate effectively without establishing a separate field support footprint, while also preserving impartiality between Iraq and Kuwait by avoiding a permanent presence in one capital.
At the same time, efforts are being made to address the challenges posed by distance and time zones and to ensure that operational modalities remain as efficient as possible. Official travel is carefully consolidated and strategically planned, with combined visits to Iraq and Kuwait aligned, to the extent possible, with meetings of the Tripartite Commission and its Technical Subcommittee calendars. Between such visits, engagement with relevant counterparts is sustained through video conferencing and other remote means, thereby supporting continuity while containing costs.
The Secretariat will continue to keep these arrangements under review, as requested by the Advisory Committee, and will provide updated information in future budget submissions, as appropriate
The Advisory Committee trusts that information on the efforts of the Senior Representative to seek extrabudgetary funding will be included in the next report of the Secretary-General. (para. 17).

The Senior Representative has been actively engaging with relevant Member States in New York, including Iraq and Kuwait. She will travel to both Iraq and Kuwait in June 2026 to meet with government officials and other interlocutors, with a view to gaining a comprehensive understanding of all aspects of the mandate and the perspectives of each side. The Senior Representative will attend the Tripartite Commission as soon as her observer status is confirmed by both sides. Participation in this forum will be instrumental in further deepening her understanding of the issues at hand, as well as the expectations of all parties.
Following several rounds of engagement with the relevant stakeholders, the Senior Representative will be in a stronger position to provide an update on any potential opportunities for extrabudgetary funding.

The Advisory Committee trusts that the Secretary-General will continue to reassess the structure, level and number of personnel of the mission support component, with a view to identifying further efficiencies commensurate with the substantially reduced operations and will present more comprehensive information on the projected workload of the mission and related staffing proposals in his next report. (para. 37)

The assessment determined that the current staffing level represents the minimum critical capacity required to sustain mandate implementation, enabling the Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Yemen can continue to meet its obligations to the Security Council, protect its personnel, and maintain the credibility and effectiveness of its political and mediation engagement. For 2027 the Office will continue to pursue efficiencies through the optimization of existing resources, while ensuring alignment with projected workload requirements.

The Advisory Committee trusts that more detailed information on the impact of the closure of UNMHA and the relocation of the position of Programme Management Officer to Aden on the provision of technical assistance to mine action bodies and its workload will be provided in the next budget report. (para. 39)

Since the deployment of the Programme Management Officer to Aden in April, numerous in-person meetings were held with the national authorities for mine action as well as the other stakeholders, including four international NGOs operating in government-controlled areas. The Programme Management Officer has played a  bridge role between the local authorities, the Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Yemen and the United Nations country team, facilitating information-sharing and validation of data, including threat analysis relating to landmines, explosive remnants of war (EWR), sea mines, and improvised explosive devices (IEDs). Engagement with the Chair of the National Mine Action Committee has supported discussions on a multi-year national mine action strategy. At the  request of the World Food Programme (WFP), three explosive ordnance risk education sessions were held, reaching 132 United Nations staff and 45 partner personnel. The coordination role of the Programme Management Officer is critical. The Programme Management Officer contributes to security planning, including discussions on road openings. The monitoring and analysis of data through third party reporting mechanisms further supports situational awareness.

The Advisory Committee trusts that the Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Yemen will reassess air transport needs based on actual workload following the transfer of residual functions to it and will continue to explore additional opportunities for cost-sharing arrangements with other entities, with information to be provided in future budget submissions. (para. 45)

The Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Yemen requires a dedicated fixed-wing aircraft to effectively implement its operational and political mandate, particularly following the transfer of residual functions from UNMHA. The Mission’s activities demand timely, flexible, and secure air transport across Yemen and the wider region, as the urgency and sensitivity of movements for the Special Envoy frequently exceed standard operational timelines. These movements are driven by ongoing mediation efforts, political engagements, and evolving security conditions, including support to prisoner exchange mechanisms, Redeployment Coordination Committee (RCC) engagements, and high-level advocacy with regional and international stakeholders. 
The aircraft provides essential operational capacity for mandate implementation, good offices engagement, and the secure transport of personnel and delegations, particularly in high-risk contexts where commercial options are unavailable. Implementation of the Office’s mandate, including responsibilities under Security Council resolution 2813 (2026), requires regular movement of staff and delegations between Amman, Sana’a, and Aden, as well as regional hubs such as Muscat and Djibouti. These missions support key activities including Military Coordination Committee meetings, ceasefire monitoring, and direct political consultations with parties and stakeholders. Sensitive political processes, notably prisoner exchange arrangements, further require the use of UN-managed or unmarked aircraft to ensure neutrality and safe participation.
In addition, the aircraft facilitates the movement of senior UN officials as well as emergency response functions such as CASEVAC/MEDEVAC, and the transport of non-UN and official delegations under UN mandate.
The operating environment in Yemen severely limits alternatives. There are no commercial flights to Sana’a, access to Aden remains unreliable, safe ground routes are absent, UNHAS operations have been suspended since early April, and regional conflict continues to disrupt aviation access. These constraints, combined with fuel supply challenges, make dedicated UN aviation assets the only viable means of sustaining operations.
Without such capacity, the Office’s ability to operate within Yemen and engage meaningfully in the political process would be significantly curtailed, undermining effective mandate delivery and limiting engagement to external actors.
